reason: The provided sources fully support a surprising, fast-paced story with well over 10 mutually corroborated atomic claims.
story: In October 1959, the Soviet Union launched Luna 3, a small probe tasked with revealing the Moon's hidden far side. Because the Moon is tidally locked, humanity had never seen the hemisphere facing away from Earth. To photograph it, Soviet engineers built an automated deep-space darkroom inside the spacecraft, using an onboard chemical processor to develop, fix, and dry the film mid-flight before scanning it with a cathode-ray tube to radio the images home. The biggest twist? The radiation-resistant 35mm film inside the camera wasn't Soviet-made—it was American film salvaged from downed US Genetrix spy balloons. The resulting grainy photos proved the far side was densely cratered and nearly devoid of dark volcanic maria, permanently altering our map of the Moon and setting the stage for modern space exploration.
angle: The Soviet Union used American spy film, salvaged from downed US reconnaissance balloons, to capture the very first photographs of the Moon's hidden far side.

claims.claim: Luna 3 was launched by the Soviet Union in October 1959.
Luna 3 was the first mission to photograph the far side of the Moon.
The Moon is tidally locked, keeping its far side permanently hidden from Earth.
The spacecraft carried the Yenisey-2 imaging system, built around a dual-lens AFA-E1 camera.
The camera carried 35mm temperature- and radiation-resistant film salvaged from downed American Genetrix espionage balloons.
Luna 3 took 29 photographs over roughly 40 minutes on 7 October 1959.
The photographs covered about 70 percent of the lunar far side.
The spacecraft contained an automated processing unit that developed, fixed, and dried the film onboard.
A flying-spot scanner using a cathode-ray tube read the developed negatives and converted them into radio signals.
Seventeen frames were successfully transmitted back to Earth.
The far side images revealed mountainous terrain and far fewer dark maria compared to the near side.
Features identified and named from the mission included Mare Moscoviense and Tsiolkovskiy crater.

disputed: The exact number of successfully transmitted frames varies slightly across accounts, with some sources citing 17 frames and others noting up to 12; scripts should use the widely cited figure of 17 or attribute it accordingly.

The origin of the American balloon film is described in some sources as a widely repeated history or possibility; scripts should frame this detail using phrasing like 'according to historical accounts'.
